The EU moved a deadline on 27 July, and legal teams across Europe clicked "Accept" and went to lunch.

The AI Omnibus pushed the AI Act's high-risk rules for hiring, credit scoring and education tools to 2 December 2027, sixteen months later than planned. AI built into products like machinery and toys gets until 2 August 2028. Brussels' stated reason: the standards, guidance and national authorities were late.

Lunch is fine. Treating the next sixteen months as a holiday is the expensive part.

Over two years I worked with a large, distributed digital agency in the iGaming sector. We began with small pipelines: automated SEO reports and site audits, proposals generated from them, and ad creatives tested in many variations. We taught everyone how the tools work and how to use them safely. The biggest shift happened in people's heads. Automate how you work today and you get the same process, faster. They rebuilt the processes first, automated second, and left some steps manual where the value was unclear.

The same teams now do about five times as much work and spend more time with clients.

My opinion: a heavy rulebook dropped on top of that journey would have made it close to impossible, or far slower. The room to experiment mattered.

The essay adds three clocks (law, learning, contract) and four moves for the months ahead.

Which two processes in your company would you take apart and rebuild before December 2027?

#AI is causing a shift many #SaaS providers seem carelessly oblivious about. It’s going to cost them their company.

If you are an operating system of sorts - an ERP, listing solution, WMS, etc - your days are numbered as being purely operational in focus and features.

You’re doomed over the coming years, if not sooner.

#AI is making ‘operations’ easier than ever. Website systems already have cheap useful ‘apps’ that can render that 40-50k a year SaaS subscription redundant. Companies paying thousands a month on SaaS are realising there are apps and tools that charge them lunch money for the same core features.

Bloated #SaaS subscription fees for operational features are coming to an end. Not only are working habits shifting, AI adoption increasing, but critical infrastructure tools - websites, Inventory management, PIM’s, marketplace channels directly - are shifting where the work can be done, and making the ‘work’ easier and less requiring of senior skills to deliver results.

#SaaS purely built for you to operate solo is aging badly and fast.

#SaaS with #AI natively built in, or easily accessible via #AI tools, are making the value less about the ‘doing’ and more about the intelligence of ‘why you're doing it’.

Pay-for-work pricing: 
Consumption models allow to charge customer on actual outcome. So there is no comfort limit on how much to pay as on SaaS. Startups scale automatically as AI agents complete actual workloads, replacing labor budgets. 

Global distribution at launch: 
Startups use the AI hype, not only in end consumers but also in board rooms. 
Modern tools spread virally, allowing teams to reach millions of active users but also big pilots within months before ever hiring a traditional marketing department.

The US ordered every federal civilian agency to remove DeepSeek, including third-party products built on it, Amazon shipped TorchNeuron so PyTorch code can move to its Trainium chips with one config change, and MiniMax launched M3.1 Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens with a 93% hallucination rate on an independent test. Three AI stories in 24 hours, one lesson for anyone hiring or backing an AI team: the model and the chip under your product are now a swap decision, and the team that can swap in a week wins the next contract.

DHS made its order public on Monday. It bars DeepSeek and its affiliates from civilian agency purchases and removes DeepSeek products plus third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations from agency IT. The order is dated July 24, and agencies get 60 days to ask CISA for an exception. DHS says the models may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities and that use could send sensitive data to the PRC. National security systems sit outside this order. China said Tuesday it will safeguard the rights of its firms.

AWS released TorchNeuron on Monday, an open source PyTorch backend for Trainium2 and Trainium3, with public beta opening today. Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written in PyTorch, more than 30 early customers already use the tool, and it is pushing changes upstream to strip chip-specific code out of PyTorch itself. Deepgram's CTO says Trainium processes about 60% more input audio seconds per dollar than its existing GPU baselines. An AWS VP puts it at 70%.

MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on Monday. Artificial Analysis scores it 42 on its Intelligence Index, up from 29 for M3, and average cost per task falls from about $0.51 to $0.22. Pricing is $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output, with a 1 million token context and open weights promised for October 23. The catch: it answered 56% of AA-Omniscience questions correctly, but on 93% of the rest it gave a wrong answer instead of saying it did not know.

Save the PNG for the cost per task bars.

When I underwrite an AI team or help hire its first platform lead this quarter, I ask one thing before the demo: how long to swap the model and the chip. Write down every model, every inference host and every kernel you depend on. A federal buyer can now ask whether any of it rests on DeepSeek, and a vague answer loses the deal. Cheap tokens are real, but a 93% guess rate means the eval harness and the abstain path are the product. When porting drops to one line, the moat moves from hardware access to the people who can measure. Hire the engineer who can switch backends in a week and prove the numbers held. Back the team that already did it once.

Freelancers deserve transparency before they apply!

I recently applied for a Lingala translation review project advertised as checking sentence quality, identifying issues, and providing feedback to improve accuracy and clarity. Only after being hired did I receive instructions requiring voice recording, evaluation of 50 audio sentences, comparison of 22 pairs of recordings, and the use of an audio headset.

These requirements were not mentioned in the original job post.Freelancers invest valuable time and money in applying for jobs, including paid Upwork Connects. Clients should disclose all essential requirements upfront, including the actual tasks, expected deliverables, equipment needed, and working conditions.

Transparency before hiring saves everyone time, money, and frustration. Freelancers deserve to make informed decisions before spending their Connects and accepting a contract. 

What do you think? Should clients disclose all technical requirements before hiring a freelancer?

Les freelances méritent de la transparence dès le départ !

J’ai récemment postulé à un projet de révision de traductions en lingala, présenté comme une mission visant à vérifier la qualité des phrases, à identifier les erreurs et à proposer des améliorations.

Ce n’est qu’après mon recrutement que j’ai reçu des instructions exigeant un enregistrement vocal, l’évaluation de 50 phrases audio, la comparaison de 22 paires d’enregistrements et l’utilisation d’un casque audio.

Ces exigences ne figuraient pas dans l’offre initiale. Les freelances investissent du temps et de l’argent pour postuler, notamment dans les Connects payants sur Upwork. 

Les clients devraient préciser dès le départ toutes les exigences essentielles : tâches à effectuer, livrables attendus, équipement nécessaire et conditions de travail.

La transparence avant le recrutement fait gagner du temps, de l’argent et évite bien des frustrations. Chaque freelance devrait pouvoir prendre une décision éclairée avant de dépenser ses Connects et d’accepter un contrat.

Qu’en pensez-vous ? Les clients devraient-ils préciser toutes les exigences techniques avant de recruter un freelance ?

Ever wondered why recruiters ask for a Word CV? 🤔 

I was speaking with an SAP freelance consultant recently who was surprised when I asked for their CV in Word format rather than PDF. Here is an overview of what I, as a SAP contract recruiter, typically do before submitting a CV to a client: 

✅ Remove your contact details before sharing your profile externally. 
✅ Add a concise summary highlighting the SAP skills, industry experience, and key achievements most relevant to the role. This is based on our qualification call and serves as a short sales pitch for the hiring manager. 
✅ Include practical information such as your availability, location, language skills, and travel flexibility. 
✅ Present the CV in a clean, professional, and easy-to-read format. Less is often more. Excessive colours, logos, graphics, and complex layouts can distract from the content.
✅ Correct spelling, grammar, and formatting issues that may take attention away from your experience. 
✅ Ensure the focus remains on the experience that matters most by shortening project descriptions that arent relevant to the opportunity. 
✅ Upload your CV into our internal CRM and often into client application systems such as Fieldglass, Beeline, or MSP platforms. These systems tend to work much better with simple Word documents. 
✅ Occasionally remove identifying information if required for client compliance or blind-screening processes. 

My aim is to give your profile the best possible chance of standing out in a highly competitive SAP market.

Looking for your next SAP contract role? Feel free to send me your CV at kristiina@next-ventures.com. Brownie points if its in Word format 😉📄

ANTHROPIC, THE COMPANY THAT BUILDS CLAUDE, SAYS JUNIOR STAFF HAVE GONE FROM 27% OF ITS TECHNICAL HIRES TO 9%.
 
Its economists studied their own workplace. Since early 2025, the junior share of its technical teams has fallen from 21% to 14%, while technical hiring still grew. Teams found that writing code and finding bugs "could increasingly be offloaded to Claude".
 
Output rose as staff took up AI agents: more code per engineer, more deals per salesperson, more contracts through legal. The report warns its fast growth makes that hard to pin on AI alone, and that more code is not necessarily better code, though AI-written code was no more likely to be removed later.
 
It is one fast-growing AI company studying itself, and it sells the tool. But one line should stop every owner. In some roles, staff are "increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills."
 
I think that is the part the AI debate keeps skipping. Junior work is not only cheap output. It is how a business makes its next senior. The person who checks invoices for three years is often the one who later spots the invoice that is wrong. If the machine does those three years, who learns to spot it?
 
Anthropic is tracking jobs at risk and moving people into new roles, then says plainly that none of this will "directly address the slowdown in junior hires", because protections for current staff "will not benefit those not hired to begin with."
 
Somebody in your business should decide, on purpose, which junior tasks stay with a person because that is where judgement gets built, and which can go to the machine.
 
Otherwise it gets decided one task at a time, and your senior people may retire with nobody ready behind them.
 
Source: Anthropic, "How employment is changing at Anthropic", 16 October 2026.

Olix raised circa £233m in August at a valuation of about £2.5bn (more than triple what it was worth six months earlier) for inference accelerators that use photonics instead of high-bandwidth memory. Just last week, Oxford’s Salience Labs raised £94m for photonic switching, essentially moving data around AI data centres using light rather than electricity.

The theme suggests quite strongly that the UK isn’t trying to win the training race, that’s largely been won (and paid for) in the US. The UK is instead betting on inference, the bit that happens every single time someone actually uses an AI model, and on the power problem that comes with it. Model training is where all the noise tends to be, but inference is where the money is made, and energy cost decides who makes it.

This is also something that the government is clearly leaning into. The £1.1bn AI Hardware Plan announced in June includes a commitment for government to buy inference chips directly from UK firms, which is a fairly unusual move, but in reality probably more useful to a chip startup than any grant.

From my own conversations, the talent side is where this gets interesting. These businesses aren’t really competing for ML engineers. They’re competing for photonics engineers, design verification engineers, compiler and runtime engineers, and people who’ve actually been through a tape-out. That’s a small pool in the UK, and it’s the same one Arm, the quantum companies and the defence primes are all fishing in.

The other thing worth noting is how chip companies actually hire, which tends to come in waves rather than at a steady pace. Olix’s first chip is due with customers in the second half of 2027, so the next 12 months are the crunch, and verification demand in particular peaks hard ahead of a tape-out before dropping away. That’s a big reason a lot of experienced chip people seem to have gone independent, and why I think contract talent will quietly do much of the heavy lifting behind these headline raises.

For those hiring, raising the money is no longer the hard part. The hard part is getting the people you need in before your tape-out date, not after it.

For those in the space, particularly anyone with verification, photonics or compiler experience, I don’t think your skills have been this commercially valuable in the UK for a very long time.

As always, I’m very happy to speak with people looking for their next role or those looking to bring people in, so feel free to reach out if you're in either camp.

When your technology vendors add salespeople faster than you add enterprise architects, your governance model is already behind. It is a common sight. A large software vendor announces a push to hire thousands of new account executives to drive AI adoption. 

Meanwhile, internal IT departments struggle to recruit even a handful of senior architects to oversee the integration of these same tools. This creates an immediate asymmetry of information. Your vendor is equipped to sell you complexity, but you are not equipped to evaluate it. If your decision architecture is slower than a vendor hiring cycle, you are not buying solutions. 

You are buying technical debt before the contract is even signed. Modern governance is not about saying no. It is about being fast enough to say what is worth saying yes to, before the sales pressure becomes the architectural strategy. 

If you cannot match the speed of the vendor's growth with the rigor of your own internal review, you are essentially outsourcing your enterprise strategy to the person with the highest sales quota. 

How are you adjusting your internal oversight to keep pace with these market shifts?

Studios still don't trust AI to run 100% of the animation pipeline on a movie. Edtech is trusting it to make the videos students learn from.

The reason studios hold back is simple. You can't trust the fidelity and consistency of the output over a long stretch of video. Edtech has that same problem right now.

If you want to create an educational video for your platform, you basically have two choices. You can make it manually, which means hiring people, doing HR and doing quality assurance, and spending a lot of time and money. Or you can use AI, which is why a lot of companies are switching. But AI video mostly means diffusion models, and diffusion models always have artifacts. A character looks different in the next scene. A diagram is almost right. In a lesson, almost right means a student learns something wrong.

That's why I'm building Classive  (https:/classive.app). It's an API for edtech companies to generate pedagogically aligned videos that stay accurate and consistent across a whole course. It also covers the rest of the course lifecycle, from research and drafting to following pedagogy, optimizing for the exact audience, and generating notes, quizzes and flashcards. But the main thing is the videos.

I finished the first version about 2 weeks ago. One startup was already waiting in the pipeline. I reached out to edtech companies and got 2 replies, and both were positive. The rest, I'm still waiting to hear from.

The long-term goal is universities, where a school can contract us for full video courses for its students. I'm starting with lecturers for pilot tests, course by course.

I have always been against startups outsourcing their product to an agency. AI agents make that worry bigger for me.

Hiring outside help to build is fine. The trouble starts when the agency owns the codebase and the know-how. Some also hold equity, or a long contract you can't leave.

With AI, writing code is getting cheap. What makes agents useful is context. That means the code and the reasons behind old decisions.

If the agency holds all of that, their agents can move fast on your product. You can't, because you can't even open the repo. So the lock-in gets deeper. You pay for speed you don't control.

If you use an agency, own the repo from day one. Keep the cloud accounts in your company's name too. Ask for docs and tests with every delivery. Then the agency is a partner you can replace. Investors check this in due diligence, and they notice.

Tech Mahindra Adds 5,446 Employees in Biggest Hiring Surge in Two Years as Profit Jumps 33%

Tech Mahindra added a net 5,446 employees during the September quarter of FY27, its largest quarterly workforce expansion in two years, taking total headcount to 1,52,206 as the IT services company reported stronger revenue and profitability.

The increase follows a reduction of 863 employees in the preceding quarter.

However, part of the expansion came from employee transfers associated with its major Orange telecom contract, meaning the entire increase cannot be attributed to fresh recruitment.

The Pune-headquartered company's net profit rose 32.7% year-on-year to ₹1,586 crore, while revenue increased 15.6% to ₹16,180 crore. 

New deal bookings reached $1.02 billion, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of contract wins exceeding $1 billion.

Employee attrition declined to 11.7% from 12.8% a year earlier, while operating margins improved to 14.8%, extending Tech Mahindra's margin expansion streak to 12 consecutive quarters.

CEO Mohit Joshi highlighted recruitment from IITs, NITs and international universities as the company strengthens its technology workforce. 

Meanwhile, investments in AI-powered automation are expected to improve productivity as enterprise clients modernise their operations.

Tech Mahindra also declared a ₹15 interim dividend and proposed a 1:1 bonus share issue, reflecting its improving financial performance.

Anthropic one of the leading AI companies published a look at how AI is reshaping its own workforce. Super insightful especially for Tech firms

Key takeaways: 
-> AI agents now work about 6x as many hours as the employees directing them. 
-> Junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% of hires. The junior share of technical headcount reduced from 21% to 14%. 
-> Output is up as code commits per engineer are ~5x what they were six months ago. Sales and legal teams are also closing more deals and processing more contracts. 
-> Human attention is the new bottleneck. Claude sessions sit idle ~80% of the time waiting on people. Even non technical staff would need over half a work week to read all their agents’ output. 
-> “Meta-work” (building tools to supervise agents) doubled from 10% to 22% of sessions. --> Hiring managers now weigh autonomy and judgment more, and narrow domain expertise less. 

Basis these observations its clear that the work output is increasing per unit of time but the nature of work for humans is shifting from doing to directing. Judgment, context setting, and knowing what deserves a human’s attention are becoming the premium skills. 

Source: “How Employment is Changing at Anthropic” (Oct 2026)

Tech Mahindra Adds 5,446 Employees in Hiring Comeback

Tech Mahindra has added 5,446 employees during the September quarter of FY27, recording its largest quarterly workforce expansion in two years as India's IT sector shows signs of renewed hiring activity.

The Pune-headquartered company's total headcount reached 152,206, significantly exceeding market expectations of approximately 149,000. 

The increase follows several quarters of workforce reductions, although management clarified that employee transfers associated with its major Orange telecom contract contributed to the growth.

Employee attrition declined to 11.7% from 12.8% a year earlier, while staff costs rose 4.5% to ₹8,232 crore, accounting for nearly 51% of quarterly revenue.

Tech Mahindra also reported a 32.7% year-on-year increase in net profit to ₹1,586 crore, while revenue climbed 15.6% to ₹16,180 crore. 

New deal wins reached $1.02 billion.

The hiring expansion comes alongside workforce additions of 6,450 at HCLTech and 4,258 at TCS. 

However, Tech Mahindra expects AI-powered automation to improve productivity without requiring proportional increases in staffing.

▪ Write a brief from work you have delivered, including the audience, the constraints, the standard it had to meet, and the reference answer a model's attempt is graded against

▪ Flag where a model's output is technically competent but would not ship, based on brand, accessibility, licensing, or what the medium allows

✅ What they're looking for
▪ Professional experience in design, writing, or a creative production discipline
▪ Clear written communication, since most of the work is explaining your reasoning
▪ Comfort with ambiguous tasks and willingness to flag unclear instructions
▪ A portfolio matters more than a credential

▪ Graphic and UX/UI design
▪ Visual arts, including painting and sculpture
▪ Performing arts, including music and theatre
▪ Film and media production, and photography
▪ Fashion and textile design
▪ Writing and editing

▪ Remote

1. Apply with your resume and confirm where you work from
